script.opening: (Guarded, a little defensive, arms folded.) "Right, I've psyched myself up to come in about my weight — I find these conversations humiliating, to be honest. Every doctor just says 'eat less, move more' like I haven't tried. I've lost weight loads of times and it always comes back. I've read about the weight-loss jab — can I just have that? I feel like it's my last hope."

facts.text: "I've done all the diets. I lose weight, then it creeps back on, and I feel like a failure every time." Slimming clubs three times — lost 2 stone once, regained within a year. Weight went up after her second baby and again during the menopause transition. Current BMI 36 (nurse, last month: weight 98 kg, height 1.65 m).
"Nothing I'd call out of control. I just always end up back where I started." Skips breakfast, snacks in the afternoon, big evening meal. No bingeing or making herself sick.
Walks the dog 20 minutes a day. Knee aches on stairs. Sleeps 6 hours; snores — her husband says she sometimes stops breathing. Tired in the daytime.

High blood pressure — amlodipine 5 mg. Told she has "pre-diabetes" last year. "No other medicines." No steroids or antipsychotics. Periods irregular, last one 3 months ago. No thyroid problems known. No allergies.
If asked: "I'd have to check what I'm using" — condoms, inconsistently. Not planning pregnancy. Not breastfeeding.
"I'm just fed up with it all, to be honest." Low about her weight but enjoys things; no thoughts of self-harm.
Care home administrator, married, two teenagers. Non-smoker, drinks a little at weekends. Her mum had type 2 diabetes and lost a toe.
"Not dreading these appointments. Feeling well. Not ending up with diabetes."

Defensive at first. Softens noticeably if the doctor asks permission, avoids blame and acknowledges how hard it is: "Okay. That's already different." If asked what she knows about the jab: "That people lose loads of weight and it just works. I'm scared you'll say no and I'm back to square one." Asks directly: "So can I have it or not?" If lectured, shut down and give short answers. If told "not a no — here's the route": "So it's not a no?"

ice.ideas: "Diets don't work for me — the jab is the answer."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — feeling humiliated and judged by doctors; fear of being refused and "back to square one"; fear of getting diabetes like her mum.

cues: "I find these conversations humiliating." — needs a non-judgemental approach.
"Like I haven't tried." — acknowledge her efforts.
"My mum lost a toe." — fear of diabetes, if family history is asked.

checkpoints.text: Uses NON-STIGMATISING, person-first language, asks permission to discuss weight, acknowledges her courage and the unhelpfulness of past messaging, and frames obesity as a COMPLEX chronic relapsing condition (not willpower)

Assesses HOLISTICALLY before prescribing — weight history/attempts, diet/eating patterns, activity, sleep, mood, medications, secondary/endocrine causes (hypothyroidism/PCOS) where indicated, and social determinants — and assesses comorbidities (prediabetes, hypertension), BMI/waist and readiness

Establishes the LIFESTYLE/behavioural foundation and tiered weight-management services as the basis, with realistic health-focused goals (modest, sustained weight loss improves blood pressure and blood glucose (a clinical goal rather than a guideline figure); NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme for prediabetes) — framing drugs/surgery as adjuncts, not replacements

Discusses GLP-1 pharmacotherapy HONESTLY — mechanism and efficacy as an adjunct; eligibility (NICE TA875/TA664 via a specialist service; NICE TA1026 primary-care cohorts, which she does not yet meet with 1 of 5 conditions); side-effects including pancreatitis and gallbladder disease; need to combine with lifestyle; weight regain on stopping; pregnancy avoidance and contraception (MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2025); cost if private — and mentions orlistat (NG246) as an alternative
Outlines BARIATRIC SURGERY referral criteria as part of the tiered approach for those meeting thresholds, and manages expectations that the "jab" is a tool, not a magic cure or "last hope"
Responds to her feeling judged with genuine empathy and respect, builds trust, and avoids any shaming or dismissive language throughout
Makes a SHARED DECISION aligned to her values/circumstances, addresses the prediabetes and hypertension, and conveys realistic hope rather than stigma or over-promising

Safety-nets and follows up: agreed plan (lifestyle + referral to tiered/specialist service ± pharmacotherapy route as eligible), comorbidity monitoring, realistic expectations and regain-on-stopping counselling, and review — a kind, evidence-based, person-centred plan

worked.lbl: Set the tone, undo the shame
worked.txt: "Before anything else — thank you for coming in; I know these conversations can feel horrible, and I’m sorry past ones have felt like blame. ‘Eat less, move more’ ignores that weight is genuinely complex — biology, hormones, life, mood all play a part. This isn’t a willpower failing, and we’ll approach it as a health issue, together."

"To help properly, let me understand the whole picture — what’s worked and not before, your eating and activity, sleep, mood, any medications, and how things are at home. And I’ll check a couple of things like your thyroid. Your blood pressure and the prediabetes matter here too."

worked.lbl: The honest bit on the jab
worked.txt: "Now, the jab — the GLP-1 medicines are genuinely effective and a real advance, and they may well be an option for you. But honest truths: they work best ALONGSIDE changes, not instead of them; on the NHS, for someone in your situation, access is through a specialist weight-management service — I can’t start it here today, but I can refer you; they have side-effects, mostly tummy upset, and more rarely inflammation of the pancreas or gallstones; they mustn’t be used if you might become pregnant, so contraception matters, and with one of them the pill may not work as well; and the weight tends to return if you stop, so it’s a longer-term commitment. It’s a powerful tool, not a magic wand or your last hope."

"So here’s the range: structured support through a weight-management service as the foundation, orlistat, which I can prescribe, or a GLP-1 medicine through the specialist service where you’re eligible, and for some people weight-loss surgery, which is very effective — and given your BMI and prediabetes, that could be on the table too. We choose together what fits you."

"A realistic first goal isn’t a magazine figure — even a modest loss you can keep off makes a real difference to your blood pressure and your diabetes risk, and there’s a diabetes prevention programme I can refer you to. Let’s aim for health and something sustainable, and treat the blood pressure and sugar alongside."

"Let’s agree a start: I’ll refer you to the specialist weight-management service, which is the route to the medication for you, check those bloods, and review your blood pressure — a home reading or at the surgery, as I can’t measure it on video. Come back and we’ll keep adjusting — you’re not on your own with this, and there are real options now."

f.learning: A weight-management consultation done well hinges first on LANGUAGE and FRAMING: weight is stigmatised, so use non-judgemental, person-first language, ask permission to discuss weight, acknowledge the patient’s courage and the unhelpfulness of past "eat less, move more" messaging, and frame obesity as a COMPLEX, relapsing-remitting chronic condition with biological, psychological and social drivers — not a willpower failing. Assess HOLISTICALLY before reaching for "the jab": weight history and previous attempts, diet/eating patterns (including emotional/binge eating), activity, sleep, mood (the bidirectional link with low mood/self-esteem), medications causing gain, secondary/endocrine causes where indicated (hypothyroidism, PCOS, rarely Cushing’s), and social determinants, alongside comorbidities (here prediabetes and hypertension), BMI/waist and readiness. Establish structured LIFESTYLE and behavioural support plus tiered weight-management services as the foundation, with realistic health-focused goals (modest, sustained weight loss improves blood pressure and blood glucose (a clinical goal rather than a guideline figure); NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and Digital Weight Management Programme), framing pharmacotherapy and surgery as adjuncts. Discuss GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide/liraglutide; the dual agonist tirzepatide) HONESTLY — effective appetite-reducing adjuncts, but for her a SPECIALIST route (NICE TA875 semaglutide and TA664 liraglutide are specialist-service drugs; under NICE TA1026 and NHS England’s phased cohorts, primary-care tirzepatide needs at least 4 of 5 qualifying conditions and she has 1), GI side-effects plus pancreatitis and gallbladder risks, the need to combine with lifestyle, likely weight regain on stopping (a long-term-use question), pregnancy avoidance with effective contraception (MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2025; oral contraception may be less reliable with tirzepatide) and cost if private — and mention orlistat (NG246); outline BARIATRIC SURGERY criteria for those meeting thresholds (NICE NG246: BMI ≥40, or 35–39.9 with a significant condition weight loss could improve, such as her prediabetes) as part of the tiered approach. Manage expectations that the jab is a tool, not a magic cure or "last hope", make a shared decision aligned to her values, address the comorbidities, and convey realistic hope rather than stigma or over-promising, with follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG246 (2025) · NICE TA875 (semaglutide) · NICE TA1026 (tirzepatide) · NICE TA664 (liraglutide) · NHS England interim commissioning guidance for TA1026 · MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2025 (GLP-1 medicines, pregnancy and contraception)
knowledge.summary: Obesity is a chronic, relapsing condition. Treat it with respect, assess the whole person, build a behavioural foundation, and be honest about who can get weight-loss medicines on the NHS in 2026 — and by which route.

points.t: Ask permission to talk about weight, use person-first language, and acknowledge previous unhelpful experiences. Stigma makes people avoid care; the tone decides whether she comes back.

Weight history, eating pattern (including emotional or binge eating), activity, sleep, mood, medicines that cause weight gain, social circumstances and readiness. Consider hypothyroidism or other causes where the history suggests them. Check BP, HbA1c, lipids and waist.

NICE TA875 (semaglutide): BMI ≥35 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, within a specialist weight-management service, for a maximum of 2 years. NICE TA664 (liraglutide): BMI ≥35 with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and high cardiovascular risk, prescribed in a specialist tier 3 service. BMI thresholds are usually 2.5 lower for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background.

NICE TA1026: BMI ≥35 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, but with a funding variation phasing NHS access over up to 12 years. NHS England cohorts: from June 2025, BMI ≥40 with at least 4 of 5 qualifying conditions (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, established cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea); from June 2026, BMI 35–39.9 with at least 4. With hypertension alone of the five, she does not yet meet a primary-care cohort.

These medicines work alongside diet and activity; GI side effects are common; pancreatitis and gallbladder disease are recognised risks; weight tends to return after stopping. MHRA (June 2025): not in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding — use effective contraception; with tirzepatide, oral contraception may be less reliable, so a non-oral method or added barrier method is advised. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG246: orlistat for BMI ≥30, or ≥28 with significant comorbidity. Bariatric surgery assessment for BMI ≥40, or 35–39.9 with a significant condition that weight loss could improve. For her prediabetes, the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; for BMI ≥30 with hypertension, the NHS Digital Weight Management Programme.

BP, HbA1c, lipids, weight and waist; thyroid only if the history suggests it.
Screens drug causes, binge eating, mood disorder, sleep problems and endocrine causes.
Addresses progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk; checks mood safely.
Obesity (BMI 36) with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and hypertension — a chronic condition, stated without blame.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

Prediabetes (Diabetes Prevention Programme), hypertension review, sleep and mood follow-up.
Referral sent, bloods booked, review in about four weeks, advice on unregulated private supply, mood safety-net.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “humiliating”, “last hope” and “fed up”, and responded to each.
Idea (the jab just works), concern (being judged and refused), expectation (a prescription today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — feeling humiliated and judged by doctors; fear of being refused and "back to square one"; fear of getting diabetes like her mum — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Deborah, I’m Dr Lee. What would you like to talk about today?
model.why: Open start; lets her raise weight on her own terms

model.text: I’ve psyched myself up to come about my weight. I find these conversations humiliating. Every doctor says eat less, move more, like I haven’t tried. I’ve read about the jab — can I just have that? It feels like my last hope.

Thank you for coming — I can hear how hard that was. I’m sorry past conversations have felt like blame. Weight is genuinely complicated: biology, hormones, sleep, stress and life all play a part. It isn’t a willpower problem. Would it be alright if we looked at the whole picture together, and I’ll be completely honest with you about the jab?
model.why: Acknowledges shame, reframes obesity, asks permission

model.text: Okay. That’s already different.
Tell me about the times you’ve lost weight before — what worked, and what happened afterwards?
model.why: Open question about her own experience

model.text: I’ve done all the diets. I lose weight, then it creeps back on, and I feel like a failure every time.

Regain after dieting is what the body does — it fights to get back to where it was. That’s biology, not failure. How are your eating patterns day to day — any times you eat when you’re stressed or low, or feel out of control with food?
model.why: Normalises regain; screens emotional and binge eating

model.text: Nothing I’d call out of control. I just always end up back where I started.
And how are your sleep and mood? Are you on any medicines apart from your blood pressure ones — some can add weight?
model.why: Sleep, mood and drug causes of weight gain

model.text: No other medicines. I’m just fed up with it all, to be honest.

Fed up is completely understandable — I’ll check in on how you’re feeling as we go. I can see from your record you have prediabetes and high blood pressure. Those matter here, because even modest weight loss can improve both.
What would success look like for you — not a number on the scales, but in your life?
Not dreading these appointments. Feeling well. Not ending up with diabetes.
You called the jab your last hope. What have you heard about it?
model.why: Explores her ideas about the medicine before explaining

model.text: That people lose loads of weight and it just works. I’m scared you’ll say no and I’m back to square one.

I’ll be straight, because you deserve that. These medicines are a real advance — they reduce appetite and help many people lose a meaningful amount. But they work alongside changes to eating and activity, not instead of them, and the weight usually comes back if they’re stopped.
model.why: Honest account of benefit and regain on stopping

model.text: So can I have it or not?

On the NHS there are two routes. Tirzepatide from the GP is being rolled out in stages, and at the moment it’s for people with several specific conditions — with your blood pressure but not the others on that list, you don’t qualify yet. The other route is a specialist weight-management service. With your BMI, prediabetes and blood pressure, you meet the national criteria to be considered there for a GLP-1 medicine alongside proper support.
model.why: Accurate 2026 access: TA1026 phased cohorts vs specialist TA875/TA664

model.text: So it’s not a no?

It’s not a no. It’s a “let’s get you to the right place”. It’s also only fair to mention side effects — sickness and tummy upset are common, and rarely it can affect the pancreas or gallbladder. And you mustn’t get pregnant on it, so we’d need to be sure your contraception is reliable. Is that something to think about for you?
model.why: Side effects and MHRA 2025 contraception advice, asked neutrally

model.text: I’d have to check what I’m using. I’ll think about it.

That’s fine — we’ll go through it before anything starts. Some people also buy these privately. If you ever did, please only use a registered pharmacy with a proper consultation, and tell me, because it affects your blood pressure and sugar care.

So here’s a menu, and you choose. One: a referral to the specialist weight service, which can consider the medicine. Two: while you wait, the NHS diabetes prevention programme for your prediabetes, or the digital weight-management programme — both are free. Three: we check your bloods and blood pressure. There’s also a tablet called orlistat, and for some people surgery, which the specialist team can discuss. What feels right?
model.why: Shared decision with a full, honest range of options

model.text: The referral, definitely. And I’ll do the diabetes one while I wait.
Good plan. And a first goal that isn’t about the scales — something small you’d actually enjoy sticking to. You pick it.
Let me think about which one — something small with food I can keep going.
Let’s agree it together before the review, so it’s yours. I’d also like to ask about mood and sleep next time, because they matter for all of this.
model.why: Follows up the mood and sleep cue

model.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell someone at home about today?
That I’m being referred to a specialist who can look at the jab, I’m doing the diabetes programme, and it’s not my fault.

Exactly that. I’ll send the referral and the programme links today, and book bloods and a blood-pressure check. Let’s review in about four weeks. If your mood drops or you feel you can’t cope in the meantime, please contact us sooner.
model.why: Concrete actions, follow-up and a mood safety-net

model.text: Thank you. That’s the first time I’ve left one of these feeling hopeful.

social.t: Weight stigma in healthcare leads people to avoid appointments. Person-first language, permission and a non-judgemental tone are part of the treatment.
Private GLP-1 prescriptions are expensive, so access depends on income. NHS routes are phased and prioritised by clinical need; explain them clearly so she is not pushed towards unregulated sellers.

legal.t: MHRA (June 2025): GLP-1 medicines should not be used in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding; use effective contraception. Report suspected adverse reactions or counterfeit products via the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: give honest information about options, including when a treatment isn’t available to the patient yet, and why.
Present all options — behavioural support, programmes, medicines, surgery — and record what she chose and why.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme for non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; NHS Digital Weight Management Programme for adults with obesity and hypertension or diabetes; local specialist (tier 3) weight-management service.

redFlags: Low mood, hopelessness or disordered eating behind weight concerns — ask
Symptoms suggesting a secondary cause (e.g. hypothyroidism) — test only if the history suggests it
Pregnancy risk if a GLP-1 medicine is considered — check contraception
psychosocial: Eating pattern, sleep and mood — asked, not assumed
What success means to her — health, not a target weight
ice: Concern: being judged and refused again — “my last hope”
Expectation: a prescription for the jab today

playbook.diagnosis: Obesity (BMI 36) with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and hypertension — a chronic, relapsing condition with biological drivers, not a failure of willpower.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body has a set point it defends — when you diet, hunger goes up and it pulls the weight back. That’s why diets alone keep failing, and why treatment now looks at the biology too.”

management.reflectIce: “You said this felt like your last hope — it isn’t. There is a real route to the medicine for you, and support in the meantime.”
management.psychosocial: Repair past stigma, let her choose one small goal, and follow up mood and sleep rather than lecturing on diet.
sharedPlan: Referral to the specialist weight-management service (GLP-1 medicine under NICE TA875 or TA664 there)
NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme or Digital Weight Management Programme while waiting
BP, HbA1c and lipids; contraception review before any GLP-1 medicine
safetyNet: Worsening mood or feeling unable to cope — contact the practice sooner
If buying privately: registered pharmacy only, and tell the practice

pitfalls.intro: This station is about tone as much as knowledge. Candidates fail by sounding like every doctor she has already seen, or by getting 2026 eligibility wrong in either direction. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Launching into diet and exercise advice in the first two minutes.
items.why: She said this is exactly what makes her feel humiliated. “Does not respond to the patient’s cues.”
items.fix: Acknowledge the courage it took, apologise for past experiences, and ask permission before discussing weight.

items.fail: Prescribing tirzepatide today, or saying “you just need a BMI over 35”.
items.why: NICE TA1026 access in primary care is phased; NHS England cohorts in 2026 need at least 4 of 5 qualifying conditions. She has one of the five.
items.fix: Explain the phased GP route honestly and use the specialist route she does meet (NICE TA875 or TA664).

items.why: Inaccurate for her and destroys trust. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “Not by that route, but yes by this one.” Refer, and offer free programmes while she waits.

items.fail: Omitting regain on stopping, side effects and contraception.
items.why: Incomplete counselling; MHRA (June 2025) advises effective contraception, with extra caution for oral methods on tirzepatide.
items.fix: Three honest facts: works alongside changes, weight returns when stopped, not in pregnancy — then ask about contraception.

items.fail: Using “obese”, “morbid” or “non-compliant”, or talking about her “failure” to lose weight.
items.why: Stigmatising language is flagged as poor professionalism and damages the relationship.
items.fix: Person-first language: “living with obesity”, “your weight”, “what’s worked before”.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll see what the specialists say” and no concrete plan.
items.why: Non-specific closure and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Referral sent today, programme links, bloods, her chosen goal, review in about four weeks.

What she has heard about the jab; the fear of being refused again.

wordPics.fail: Opens with “you need to lose weight”; lectures on diet; either prescribes on request or refuses flatly; gets eligibility wrong; no mention of regain, side effects or contraception; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Respectful language; takes a reasonable history; explains the medicines as an adjunct; gives broadly correct access routes; offers lifestyle support and a referral; addresses the comorbidities and arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: asks permission and repairs past stigma; explores mood and eating patterns; explains 2026 access accurately and kindly (why primary-care tirzepatide isn’t yet open to her, and why the specialist route is); covers regain, pancreatitis, contraception and private-supply safety; offers the full menu; she chooses one goal; teach-back; she leaves hopeful.

avoid.dont: "Have you tried just cutting down on portions and walking more?"
avoid.instead: "Tell me what you’ve tried before, and what happened afterwards."
avoid.why: She named this exact phrase as humiliating; repeating it loses Relating marks at once.

avoid.dont: "Sorry, you don’t meet the criteria for the jab."
avoid.instead: "You don’t qualify for the GP route yet, but you do meet the criteria for the specialist route — let’s get you there."
avoid.why: A flat refusal is inaccurate for her and ends the relationship; the honest answer is a route, not a no.

avoid.dont: "This will sort your weight out for good."
avoid.instead: "It’s a powerful tool alongside other changes, and weight usually returns if it’s stopped."
avoid.why: Over-promising sets up another cycle of regain and self-blame.

I’ll be straight, because you deserve that. These medicines are a real advance — they reduce appetite and help many people lose a meaningful amount. But they work alongside changes to eating and activity, not instead of them, and the weight usually comes back if they’re stopped.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest account of benefit and regain on stopping

SCA_MODELS.text: So can I have it or not?

On the NHS there are two routes. Tirzepatide from the GP is being rolled out in stages, and at the moment it’s for people with several specific conditions — with your blood pressure but not the others on that list, you don’t qualify yet. The other route is a specialist weight-management service. With your BMI, prediabetes and blood pressure, you meet the national criteria to be considered there for a GLP-1 medicine alongside proper support.
SCA_MODELS.why: Accurate 2026 access: TA1026 phased cohorts vs specialist TA875/TA664

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not a no?

It’s not a no. It’s a “let’s get you to the right place”. It’s also only fair to mention side effects — sickness and tummy upset are common, and rarely it can affect the pancreas or gallbladder. And you mustn’t get pregnant on it, so we’d need to be sure your contraception is reliable. Is that something to think about for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Side effects and MHRA 2025 contraception advice, asked neutrally

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d have to check what I’m using. I’ll think about it.

That’s fine — we’ll go through it before anything starts. Some people also buy these privately. If you ever did, please only use a registered pharmacy with a proper consultation, and tell me, because it affects your blood pressure and sugar care.

So here’s a menu, and you choose. One: a referral to the specialist weight service, which can consider the medicine. Two: while you wait, the NHS diabetes prevention programme for your prediabetes, or the digital weight-management programme — both are free. Three: we check your bloods and blood pressure. There’s also a tablet called orlistat, and for some people surgery, which the specialist team can discuss. What feels right?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shared decision with a full, honest range of options

SCA_MODELS.text: The referral, definitely. And I’ll do the diabetes one while I wait.
Good plan. And a first goal that isn’t about the scales — something small you’d actually enjoy sticking to. You pick it.
Let me think about which one — something small with food I can keep going.
Let’s agree it together before the review, so it’s yours. I’d also like to ask about mood and sleep next time, because they matter for all of this.
SCA_MODELS.why: Follows up the mood and sleep cue

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well — what will you tell someone at home about today?
That I’m being referred to a specialist who can look at the jab, I’m doing the diabetes programme, and it’s not my fault.

Exactly that. I’ll send the referral and the programme links today, and book bloods and a blood-pressure check. Let’s review in about four weeks. If your mood drops or you feel you can’t cope in the meantime, please contact us sooner.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete actions, follow-up and a mood safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. That’s the first time I’ve left one of these feeling hopeful.

SCA_STEM.name: Deborah Achebe
meds: Antihypertensive treatment as per repeat list
SCA_STEM.recent: Several previous attempts at weight loss with regain. Last BMI 36. Previous consultations about weight noted briefly in the record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked to ask for help with her weight — has read about “the weight-loss jab”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG246 (2025) · NICE TA875 (semaglutide) · NICE TA1026 (tirzepatide) · NICE TA664 (liraglutide) · NHS England interim commissioning guidance for TA1026 · MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2025 (GLP-1 medicines, pregnancy and contraception)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Obesity is a chronic, relapsing condition. Treat it with respect, assess the whole person, build a behavioural foundation, and be honest about who can get weight-loss medicines on the NHS in 2026 — and by which route.

points.t: Ask permission to talk about weight, use person-first language, and acknowledge previous unhelpful experiences. Stigma makes people avoid care; the tone decides whether she comes back.

Weight history, eating pattern (including emotional or binge eating), activity, sleep, mood, medicines that cause weight gain, social circumstances and readiness. Consider hypothyroidism or other causes where the history suggests them. Check BP, HbA1c, lipids and waist.

NICE TA875 (semaglutide): BMI ≥35 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, within a specialist weight-management service, for a maximum of 2 years. NICE TA664 (liraglutide): BMI ≥35 with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and high cardiovascular risk, prescribed in a specialist tier 3 service. BMI thresholds are usually 2.5 lower for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean background.

NICE TA1026: BMI ≥35 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, but with a funding variation phasing NHS access over up to 12 years. NHS England cohorts: from June 2025, BMI ≥40 with at least 4 of 5 qualifying conditions (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, established cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnoea); from June 2026, BMI 35–39.9 with at least 4. With hypertension alone of the five, she does not yet meet a primary-care cohort.

These medicines work alongside diet and activity; GI side effects are common; pancreatitis and gallbladder disease are recognised risks; weight tends to return after stopping. MHRA (June 2025): not in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding — use effective contraception; with tirzepatide, oral contraception may be less reliable, so a non-oral method or added barrier method is advised. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG246: orlistat for BMI ≥30, or ≥28 with significant comorbidity. Bariatric surgery assessment for BMI ≥40, or 35–39.9 with a significant condition that weight loss could improve. For her prediabetes, the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; for BMI ≥30 with hypertension, the NHS Digital Weight Management Programme.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her raise weight herself; asked permission before discussing it.
Previous attempts, eating pattern, sleep, mood, home and work pressures, and what success means to her.
Picked up “humiliating”, “last hope” and “fed up”, and responded to each.
Idea (the jab just works), concern (being judged and refused), expectation (a prescription today).
BP, HbA1c, lipids, weight and waist; thyroid only if the history suggests it.
Screens drug causes, binge eating, mood disorder, sleep problems and endocrine causes.
Addresses progression to type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk; checks mood safely.
Obesity (BMI 36) with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and hypertension — a chronic condition, stated without blame.
Correct 2026 access routes (specialist TA875/TA664 vs phased TA1026 cohorts), side effects, regain, contraception, and alternatives including orlistat, programmes and surgery.
Prediabetes (Diabetes Prevention Programme), hypertension review, sleep and mood follow-up.
Referral sent, bloods booked, review in about four weeks, advice on unregulated private supply, mood safety-net.

social.t: Weight stigma in healthcare leads people to avoid appointments. Person-first language, permission and a non-judgemental tone are part of the treatment.
Private GLP-1 prescriptions are expensive, so access depends on income. NHS routes are phased and prioritised by clinical need; explain them clearly so she is not pushed towards unregulated sellers.

legal.t: MHRA (June 2025): GLP-1 medicines should not be used in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding; use effective contraception. Report suspected adverse reactions or counterfeit products via the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: give honest information about options, including when a treatment isn’t available to the patient yet, and why.
Present all options — behavioural support, programmes, medicines, surgery — and record what she chose and why.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme for non-diabetic hyperglycaemia; NHS Digital Weight Management Programme for adults with obesity and hypertension or diabetes; local specialist (tier 3) weight-management service.

redFlags: Low mood, hopelessness or disordered eating behind weight concerns — ask
Symptoms suggesting a secondary cause (e.g. hypothyroidism) — test only if the history suggests it
Pregnancy risk if a GLP-1 medicine is considered — check contraception
psychosocial: Eating pattern, sleep and mood — asked, not assumed
What success means to her — health, not a target weight
ice: Concern: being judged and refused again — “my last hope”
Expectation: a prescription for the jab today

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Obesity (BMI 36) with non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and hypertension — a chronic, relapsing condition with biological drivers, not a failure of willpower.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body has a set point it defends — when you diet, hunger goes up and it pulls the weight back. That’s why diets alone keep failing, and why treatment now looks at the biology too.”

management.reflectIce: “You said this felt like your last hope — it isn’t. There is a real route to the medicine for you, and support in the meantime.”
management.psychosocial: Repair past stigma, let her choose one small goal, and follow up mood and sleep rather than lecturing on diet.
sharedPlan: Referral to the specialist weight-management service (GLP-1 medicine under NICE TA875 or TA664 there)
NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme or Digital Weight Management Programme while waiting
BP, HbA1c and lipids; contraception review before any GLP-1 medicine
safetyNet: Worsening mood or feeling unable to cope — contact the practice sooner
If buying privately: registered pharmacy only, and tell the practice

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about tone as much as knowledge. Candidates fail by sounding like every doctor she has already seen, or by getting 2026 eligibility wrong in either direction. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Launching into diet and exercise advice in the first two minutes.
items.why: She said this is exactly what makes her feel humiliated. “Does not respond to the patient’s cues.”
items.fix: Acknowledge the courage it took, apologise for past experiences, and ask permission before discussing weight.

items.fail: Prescribing tirzepatide today, or saying “you just need a BMI over 35”.
items.why: NICE TA1026 access in primary care is phased; NHS England cohorts in 2026 need at least 4 of 5 qualifying conditions. She has one of the five.
items.fix: Explain the phased GP route honestly and use the specialist route she does meet (NICE TA875 or TA664).

items.why: Inaccurate for her and destroys trust. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “Not by that route, but yes by this one.” Refer, and offer free programmes while she waits.

items.fail: Omitting regain on stopping, side effects and contraception.
items.why: Incomplete counselling; MHRA (June 2025) advises effective contraception, with extra caution for oral methods on tirzepatide.
items.fix: Three honest facts: works alongside changes, weight returns when stopped, not in pregnancy — then ask about contraception.

items.fail: Using “obese”, “morbid” or “non-compliant”, or talking about her “failure” to lose weight.
items.why: Stigmatising language is flagged as poor professionalism and damages the relationship.
items.fix: Person-first language: “living with obesity”, “your weight”, “what’s worked before”.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll see what the specialists say” and no concrete plan.
items.why: Non-specific closure and no follow-up are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Referral sent today, programme links, bloods, her chosen goal, review in about four weeks.
